title: Sojun Mel Weitsman on Breathing
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer reads Sojun Mel Weitsman's words on breathing at the opening of a Zoom sesshin, after remembering two priests lost since the sangha last sat together: Jay Semino and Mel, who died in January. Mel's text calls breath the link between inside and outside, a friend to treat warm-heartedly, and something to keep low in the hara, even while reading the newspaper. Mel describes sitting beside the dying Maylee Scott, who lay breathing day after day, being breathed by the world. Norman adds a practice of counting exhales from one to ten, then asks everyone to bring that attention to meals, walking, and washing their faces during the week.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Morning everybody.
Welcome to zazen.
It's really nice to see everybody.
I quite missed you in this pandemic.
We don't see each other.
So, seeing all the faces on the screen, it feels like I'm coming home.
It was great this morning to sit and chant together.
That also felt like home.
I bet you're like me.
You didn't think that after having zazen online last year, we would be having it again online this year.
Who would have expected that, right?
And I hope that we're not online again next year.
I hope that by next year, we can sit again in person.
I guess it does teach us that we can't count on anything, which the Buddha taught us from the very beginning.
So, this should not really come as a surprise to us practitioners.
We live in a world in which absolutely nothing can be counted on, and this is the world that we take joy in, the world in which we see depth and beauty.
That's been our practice from the start.
We always say at the beginning of zazen that the word zazen does not mean retreat.
To say zazen retreat is actually not at all correct.
We don't have retreats in zazen.
The word zazen means to gather the mind, and we know that the world, the mind, is inside and also outside.
We know that what we think of as our mind and our thoughts is as much outside of us as it is inside of us.
It comes from outside, is outside as much as inside.
So, in other words, we realize that there's no world and there's no mind, as if these things were different things.
That's why we can't go on retreats: there's nothing to retreat from and there's nowhere to retreat to.
So, zazen is not a retreat, because we're just sitting right here, where we always are anyway.
And yes, it's a little different, of course.
We're a little bit more quiet and we make life a little more simple.
As Tim put it last night, we take a pause, that's true, but it's not a retreat really.
And I think that this is a group of very seasoned practitioners, so I don't think we need to tell you how to make the best use of this Zoom zazen.
Each one is going to find how to do that differently, depending on your circumstances, your conditions.
So, as I enter this zazen, I'm thinking very much and have very much in my heart two great Zen priests that we have lost since the last time we sat zazen together.
I hope that you know about these losses, and I'm not shocking you by telling you for the first time about them.
Maybe some of you know Jay Semino, Yu-jo, Rin-jo, courageous completion, bright presence, who died at home in San Francisco on May the 2nd.
I knew Jay a long, long time.
We were young Dharma students together in the 1970s, and Jay was ordained in a big group of people before I was ordained in the late 1970s.
He was one of the dearest people you could ever meet, kind, patient.

So, we practiced together for a long time in the heyday of the exciting times of the Zen Center, and then later on he became a builder, because he had trained as a carpenter at the Zen Center, among other things.
And then he came back to practicing Zen and became my disciple, and I gave him Dharma transmission in 2012, so we were very close.
And Jay had a particularly terrible form of Parkinson's disease that really caused him a tremendous amount of suffering, more than you think of when people have Parkinson's as bad as it is.
Jay had it very bad, and no medication would help as it got worse and worse.
He even had that brain implant procedure, which made the situation worse.
So, when he passed, it was a kind of a blessing.
It ended a nightmare life for Jay.
Although, as always, he had some joy, too, in those last years, and there was lots and lots and lots of love.
So, it wasn't a tragic situation, but it was not an easy one.
It was pretty hard, and it was hard, if you love Jay, to watch his suffering.
So, during this sesshin, I'll have Jay with me.
He was such a warm person.
He was loved by so many people.
He was actually, you knew him, a very handsome fellow, big and tall and lean, dark hair and complexion, beautiful smile.
His funeral will take place in the Bay Area a couple of days after sesshin.
I had to do some preparations for it before sesshin, and we'll have a Zoom link for the funeral.
But also, many of us who are fully vaccinated will be able to safely gather together in person to have the funeral.
So, I think we're really going to appreciate that being together.

The other great priest that we have lost is my teacher and Cathy's teacher, Hakuryu Sojun Mel Weitsman, who was the abbot of the Berkeley Zen Center since the beginning of the Berkeley Zen Center in the late 1960s.
And that's where Cathy and I met.
We met at the same time at the Berkeley Zen Center and also in a sutra class at the University of California at Berkeley, and we practiced with Mel in the Berkeley Zen Center.
In those days, it was a very small, close-knit group, so we were very close, all of us who practiced there.
That was until we went to Tassajara in 1976, and we both received Dharma transmission from Mel, me in 1988 and Cathy in 2011.
And we were very close personally with Mel and his wife Liz.
We would have annual birthday dinners together.
And although we didn't see each other all the time, he was busy in Berkeley and I was busy over here, we were always, always in touch.
And he died on January 7th at the age of 91.

It was the great fortune of his life to have found a great Zen teacher, Suzuki Roshi, and to focus his life on his teacher, studying with his teacher until that teacher died, and then to keep on practicing steadily and simply his whole life through until the very end.

I guess, I don't remember whether it was 2018 or 19, he was at Tassajara, in that rigorous practice environment at his age, happy as a clam, doing Dharma transmission ceremonies, which are very involved and complicated.
He was in the middle of that and somebody noticed he looked weird, he didn't look good.
So he was taken to the hospital and it turned out that he had cancer.
He lived pretty well, pretty comfortably with that cancer.
He was actually probably the happiest I've ever seen him in those last years with cancer.
And he was active.
He was still the abbot of the Berkeley Zen Center, going to the center all the time, practicing every day, all the way up until maybe two weeks before he passed.
Then he got too sick to do anything, so he stayed in bed and died at home, as I said.
His life, which he was writing about (he was writing a kind of memoir just when he died), was very exciting and various.
He lived through the Great Depression, and as a kid he used to go sneak into the backlots of 1930s Hollywood.
He joined the Marines on active duty.
He was a beatnik artist in North Beach, when North Beach was the center of the beatnik world, and then he started practice.
And then after that, nothing happened for the next 50 or 60 years.
Just the ordinary everyday life of a Zen priest.
He had a lot of disciples.
He gave dharma gifts to many, many people.
His practice was very firm, very definite, very down-to-earth, very faithful, very beautiful.
So I will also be sitting next to Mel during this sesshin.
He was my friend and my teacher and my foundation and my support for pretty much 50 years.
And when you're over 90, death is never unexpected, so it wasn't a shock, and I will miss him, of course.
But also, I won't, because my life is dharma, and my dharma was formed by him.
So in some way, that's very real to me, he's always with me.
Anyway, thinking of him this morning, I thought that for the rest of my talk, I will share with you his words.
He gave a talk some years ago on breathing.
Besides his memoir, he was working on a collection of his talks that will be published.
He never published any books in his lifetime, but I think there'll be a collection of his talks, maybe with the memoir at some point.
But I thought for sesshin, breathing is such an important friend, so let's appreciate together what Mel has to say about breathing.
And as you'll see from his talk, like most of his talks, he's not commenting on a text or commenting on teachings, he's just talking from his own experience.
So this is Mel on breathing.
*In Buddhist meditation, paying attention to breathing is one of the most important factors.
Breathing is usually taken for granted because it is so constant.
The blood runs through our veins.
We don't see it, but we are aware of it as heat, and we take it for granted.
Breath is something that is going on continuously.

It connects inside and outside, so to speak, because, of course, the air we take in inside of us that revitalizes our life comes from the outside, and then we return it, altered, [unclear: "back to Mel"].
Each one of us has this experience of breath.
Coming in, going out, inhaling, exhaling, this is the fundamental movement of our life.
In zazen, we pay attention to posture, and we pay attention to breath.
Posture first, because posture is the fundamental structure of this body.
After we establish posture, we pay attention to breath.
So zazen is harmonizing body, mind, and breath, all three elements.*
So I often say, now I'm commenting on that, I often say that when you think about it, that's life: body, breath, mind.
That's the fundamental bottom line of being alive.

So when we're sitting in zazen, we're returning to the fundamental bottom line of being alive, which we assume and totally forget about the rest of the time, and we are only aware of our problems and our issues and this and that that we're worried about and concerned about, but we don't ever think, oh my god, I'm alive, what's that like?
So that's zazen: body, breath, mind, life.
Back to Mel.
*If you have been sitting zazen for a while, you have this experience, but one important factor that is easy to ignore is the role of breath, or how we pay attention to breathing in our daily life.
In zazen, we let go of the busyness of our daily activity, all the complications, and it's pretty easy to simply pay attention to the rising and falling of our breath.
In our daily life, it's much more difficult.
When paying attention to the breath and sitting up straight, the breath becomes more subtle, and we then experience a feeling of liberation, lightness, settledness, freedom, and selflessness.*
So that's why zazen is so great, right?
Because we just sit and we're not trying to do anything, but pretty soon we feel that way: liberation, lightness, settledness, freedom, selflessness.
We really don't have to worry about ourselves anymore during zazen, which is such a burden, right?
Worrying about oneself.
Oh god, do we really have to do that?
Back to Mel.
*This kind of attention to the breath can be applied to all our activities when you walk, to be attentive to the breath with each step.*
During zazen, not only during kinhin, but even anytime we're walking back and forth, we can stay with our breathing.
It's a good training.
Stay with your breathing not only when you're in kinhin, but when you're walking to the kitchen or the bathroom.
He says when you're hiking, it's pretty easy.
Sometimes when you're hiking up a steep mountain, it can be one breath, one step.
*But in our daily life of varied activities, it's much more difficult to be aware of breath in your work, to be aware of breath while sitting down at your computer.
How you actually breathe with the activity and the rhythm of the breath and the activity.
Driving a car, turning on the ignition, the rhythm of shifting gears in the days when most people had gears to shift, putting on the brake, stepping on the gas.
You do that all with your breath.
To actually pay attention to breath and the movement in this way is how we carry our meditation practice into our daily life.
It is an activity that is common to both zazen and daily life.*
Suzuki Roshi said in a talk:
*We should be kind with ourselves and very kind with our breathing.
We should have a warm-hearted feeling toward our breath.*
And I hope you have a chance to develop that warm-hearted, friendly relationship to your breath during zazen.
The breath is so wonderful.
It really is.
It's so profound and so beautiful.
And it really is your best friend, to think of the breath as a friend and know that it's always there, even in times of trouble.
So he goes on:
*To develop that closeness to the breath is one of the things that happens to us when zazen practice is part of our personal culture.
We can relate to our breath as a constant companion, not simply taking it for granted.
To have this awareness focuses our attention and helps us to be concentrated on what we are doing.*
*It's the kind of energy that's not chattery, sorry, but calm and collected and creates a joyful mood.
When we can keep coming back to the breath, then our disposition actually becomes sweet and smooth and makes it easy to smile.
It helps us to respond to circumstances rather than just reacting.
It's important to keep the breath down low in your hara.
Breath in Japanese is called ki, in Chinese chi, in Sanskrit prana.
So ki or chi is the place of power or strength.
When our breath is down here in what feels like our lower abdomen, our center, just at the bottom of our lungs, we feel it just below our navel.
And this is called the sea of chi or the key of sea,* he said.
That was his joke.
In the parenthesis in my text here it says "laughter."
So ha ha, we should all have the key of sea.
*Sea of ki, the key of sea.
Suzuki Roshi said it's also called rice paddies, which in the Asian way of thinking means place of plenty, nourishment, the source of our energy and well-being.
You notice when you hyperventilate, it creates a feeling of euphoria, and when we put on an oxygen mask and take a hit of oxygen, we feel high.
In zazen, it's not necessarily to breathe in a special way; we're just breathing naturally is fine.
But often we find ourselves breathing up in our chest when we're angry or irritated or frightened or anxious.
Then our breath gets shallow and we lose our center or ground.
So when we pay attention to breathing and allow ourselves to breathe deeply, then the body relaxes and lets go of holding onto itself, and our state of mind becomes free.
Our state of mind and our breath are very connected.
That's why it's so important to harmonize body, mind and breath and resume our natural state of mind, which is free from conditioning.
In our daily lives, we meet many conditions.
All we have to do is read the newspaper to drive breathing up into our chest.
When you read the newspaper, let your breath go down to your hara and harmonize with body and mind.*
So that's a great practice, right?
Every time you read the news, think first and breathe in your belly.
*He says, even though the world looks like it's going to hell, you can still have a calm mind.
You still have your composure.
You don't get lost.*
Although Mel would sometimes get quite exasperated when he read the newspaper.
I think he would have to remind himself to go back to his breathing.
*Breathing is a kind of involuntary activity.
It has a voluntary aspect, but it is also involuntary because breath is just coming and going, regardless of our desire.
We can control the breath.
We can hold our breath for a little while or we can control the rhythm.
But in zazen and in our daily life, just allow the breath to do its own thing, and our mind follows the breath.
In zazen, we start out by letting the mind follow the breath.
This is difficult.
Once you focus on the breath, it's hard not to feel that you're controlling it.
First we say, count the breath.
That's good for getting a handle on following it.
And then just let the mind follow the breath.
Let the breath be.
Actually, we are breathed by the universe.
This is just a universal activity which is inflating and deflating the lungs.
We think usually I am breathing, but no, actually breathing is just happening to you.*

And just to inject here a thought: since going down to Tassajara a couple of years ago and studying again Zhiyi's text about the subtle dharma gates, the six subtle dharma gates, I've started again, after many years, going back to counting my breathing on the exhale from one to ten.
And sometimes people think that's a beginner's practice, and Mel almost implies that here, but it's a great practice.
It's very profound actually to count the breath from one to ten.
It's a great thing to develop in zazen if you want to.
So I recommend you might try counting the exhales from one to ten and beginning again with one, and of course starting again with one whenever you lose count.
Back to Mel.
*Breathing is a wonderful mystery.
To inhale is to come to life as we know it, and to exhale is to let go of life as we know it.
Suzuki Roshi talked about the breath at the exhale as letting go.
Long breath, letting go.
We put more attention on the exhale than the inhale.
When you inhale the body becomes excited, and when you exhale the body becomes calm.
And these are two aspects of our life, excitement and calmness.
Someone said a movement and a rest, over and over again, over and over again.
And each breath is a moment of birth and death.
This is how we can understand how our life continues.
It's both continuous and discontinuous.
Last week when I was in Arcata with our dear Dharma sister, Maylee Scott.*
I forget what year she died, but it was a long time ago, maybe in the 1990s.
And Maylee was a very dear person in our life.
Kathy, when she was a college student, lived in Maylee and Peter Scott's house to help take care of children and cook meals, in exchange for room and board.
And so we knew Maylee before she became a priest, and she became a really wonderful, important, socially active Zen Buddhist priest who was also Mel's disciple.
Anyway, now Mel talks about being with her in Arcata at the time of her dying.
*So, when I was in Arcata with our dear Dharma sister, Maylee Scott, who was dying for one week, six days, she was kind of gone.
Lying in bed on her back, not moving for all that time with her eyes closed, just breathing.
And we would go in and sit with her.
The only movement was her breath, which was quite audible.
Sometimes calm, sometimes labored.
She was breathing, but it was just the universal activity making this movement.
It was so obvious.
And we would do zazen with her and just watch to see if it would continue and to see if it would stop.
It just kept going on like this day after day, breath after breath, life living itself out.

I feel sure that her great, long experience of zazen was simply continuing, lying still, giving herself over to the universe, one with her breath, and at the right moment just stopping and experiencing this wonderful feeling of release.
I wondered how we would all feel at this moment.
And yet it was like a last breath.
And then I was sitting there also with Mel when he was in the same state, unconscious and just breathing.
Not breathing, but being breathed by the world.
The same thing, you know, he was very close and you thought, is this the last?
And then another comes.
Is this the last?
And then another comes.
Very simple.
Sometimes a moment of feeling troubled, sometimes very, very peaceful for a long time.*
Mel goes on:
*This is how I think about that time and about breathing and about appreciating our breath, not just taking it for granted, harmonizing our breath in order to allow ourselves to have that release.
In the sutra on the mindfulness of breathing, there are 16 methods of observing the breath or practicing with the breath.

And the last one, practicing with the breath in order to understand impermanence, in order to realize impermanence, and to practice letting go of body and mind so that the whole life is lived consciously and our entire death is lived consciously in the same manner.
We tend to grab on to life and resist our death, which is normal and natural.
But to live a complete life, to be able to pass out of this world in a conscious, purposeful way is possible.*
So I bet you didn't think of practicing sesshin as training for dying.
But it's really good training for dying.

The more you are friends with your breath, and that's not something you consciously figure out with your personality, but your whole body is friends with your breath, then it's going to be friends to the end.
Even if you don't have consciousness, even if you're completely unconscious, you can breathe with a sense of well-being.
Anyway, I hope that's true.
We'll find out.
We'll see.
I'll let you know.
He goes on to say:

*We can see death as losing our life, as losing something, or we can see it as gaining something, or we can see it as neither losing nor gaining, but simply expanding into the universe, which is our true body.
So paying attention to breath from the hara throughout every activity is our practice.
Sometimes I ask a student, right now, tell me, where is your breath?
And most people say, well, I don't know.
But you should know all the time where your breath is, where you are breathing from.
There shouldn't be any hesitation.
We don't know everything.
We have fears and uncertainty, and a lot of the time in our life we are puzzled by what confronts us, and our breath becomes shallow.
When we accept, I don't know, and put our mind down here in our hara, our belly, then from here something will come forth.
And this is to have faith in our true nature.
As a Zen student, you must have faith in your true nature, and it's right there in the letting go.
It's right there on every single exhale.
You can let go and have a free fall into Buddha's hand, which will always catch you.
So when we practice with our breath, settled in the hara, we have the right foundation for all our activities.
And even though we get lost, there is always a place to come back to.*
So that's what Mel has to say about breathing, at least in that one talk.
So I hope you will, so I hope you will really focus this week on your breathing.
We have a Dharma talk every day, and maybe we bring up teachings, and we think about teachings, or we think about the practice.
And our minds are thinking machines, so we have to think some.
We might as well think about Dharma as much as anything else.
But our practice is not thinking about our practice.
Our practice is in our body, in our breathing.
It's in our hands, in our feet, in our spine.
It's in our five senses, what we see and hear and taste.
So please take good care with your meals.
We're not eating oryoki meals together or eating together at a table, as we have done in the past, in silence.

So make your own discipline of paying attention to your food and looking at it and tasting it, to your walking, to your washing your face, washing your body, wearing your clothes, the feeling of being alive, knowing how swiftly life passes, and how mysterious it actually is on every breath, and just living that, without doing anything or having any big insights about it, but just feeling it every moment of sesshin.
And that's what we're here to do.
It's good that now we all have to find our own maturity, right?
We can't depend on our being together in the same space, which is so helpful and so inspiring.
We miss it, but now we all have to find a way to make that sesshin in our own space.
And looking at my screen here and seeing all of you and knowing all of you well, I know that you can all do that, and we'll do that.
It will be different from the feeling of sesshin together, but also that thread that we pick up, that thread of our practice, will be the same.
So again, I'm really happy to see all of you.
I'm really happy for this week of sesshin.
I want to thank Tim and Chris and Kate and everybody and John and everybody at Red Cedar.
I don't know, I'm sorry for all the people whose names I missed who did all the work to make this happen.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you.
I really, really appreciate your steadfast practice all these years.
We don't have a big establishment.
Other religions that are older in America have big establishments, and so there's a lot of support.
We barely even get paid, those of us who are responsible for the practice full-time.
We would barely even survive.
So it's dedication and love for the Dharma that keeps us going, which I think is good for us.
So thank you all very much for your dedication.

And I'm going to, rather than give you a headache as my computer moves across the room, I'm going to turn it off, turn off the video, and put it back in front of my altar, and then I'll do the three prostrations.
But first we'll chant the vows.
*Things are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
